samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn 'validate' into a narrower decision and warn that stated interest doesn't predict purchase. A's plan fits the time available better: 5–6 owner calls, 2–3 sitter calls, one mock screen within the designer's 3 hours a week, findings reported as 'n of N', and a clear list of what the user must do personally. B packs 8–10 owner calls, 3–4 sitter calls and an engineering fake-door test into two weeks, uses an example take-rate threshold ('above 5%') that reads like a made-up benchmark, and never sets out the human-only steps as clearly as A. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B fits the real limits better. It keeps the designer to 3 hours a week, leaves the fake door as a next step after legal review instead of squeezing an engineering build into two weeks, and lists plainly which steps the PM must do. It also warns against percentages at this sample size. A has good thinking on the decision and on feasibility, but its 5% take-rate threshold reads like an invented benchmark, its designer-hour sums are muddled, and it never clearly says which tasks a human has to do.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers start from the decision the VP needs to make, use existing data before interviews, and caution that stated interest is weak evidence. B is stronger on the rubric because it says interviews cannot show willingness to pay, lists which steps a person must do, and gives a time budget that fits the 3-hours-a-week limit. It also explains why a few conversations plus real data beat a survey. A is solid, but it is less explicit about who does what and says less about why its methods beat the alternatives. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers focus on the decision, start with existing data, use short interviews about past behaviour, and warn that stated intent overstates purchase. A is more disciplined about fitting the stated limits: it has an hours table that keeps the designer within budget, a clear split between what data and what conversations can answer, an explicit list of steps a human must do, and a fallback if recruiting falls short. B is stronger on asking the VP directly what they need and on checking partner feasibility, but it pushes a live fake-door test harder and is less explicit about who has to do what.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A names the decision the research feeds (roadmap plus partner and legal effort), says in advance what result would change the plan, and gives a dated day-by-day schedule with a clear section on what the user must do themselves. Answer B is also strong: it adds useful feasibility questions on regulation, economics and overlap with any existing guarantee. However, it ties less clearly to a specific decision, stretches the designer to about 6 hours in week 2 when they have about 3 a week, and says less plainly which steps a human has to do. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B states the decision the research feeds (whether to put the add-on on the roadmap and spend partner and legal effort on it) and says what result would change the plan. It also separates what the data can answer from what only calls can, and lists plainly what the user must do themselves. A is solid and practical, with good data mining, interviews and a fake door, but it never names the decision as clearly, has no explicit section on human-owned steps, and doesn't flag that showing an insurance price may need legal review before the fake-door test runs.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are single paragraphs of about 92–93 words with no lists. Each correctly contrasts a usability test, where a few people are observed to learn why things go wrong, with an A/B test, which compares two versions on a metric across many live users to find which wins. Neither adds a preamble, a closing offer or invented figures, and the differences in wording are cosmetic. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (about 92 and 93) with no lists, preamble or closing offer. Both correctly say a usability test is a small qualitative study that shows why people struggle, and an A/B test compares two live versions on a metric across many users to show which wins. The differences are only in wording, such as A's 'Designers often use' versus B's 'Think of', and neither invents statistics.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (A is about 99, B about 93), and both explain the why-versus-which distinction correctly. B ends with a useful summary of when to use each method. A ends with "thousands of people", a loose figure that could read as a size requirement, and a tacked-on line about good teams using both. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are a single paragraph, are accurate, and stay under 100 words, with A at about 94 words and B at about 99. A ends on a clear summary of what each test is for. B says 'complete tasks', which is slightly more precise, but it adds the loose 'thousands of people' figure and an unrequested closing line ('Good product teams use both together') that takes it right up to the word limit.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (A has about 99 and B about 94), and both explain the qualitative 'why' versus quantitative 'which' split accurately without adding a preamble or closing offer. B says 'thousands of live users', a vague sample-size figure that could read as a requirement, while A's 'many users' avoids that. B's italic contrast between *why* and *which* is a little clearer, but A follows the rubric slightly more closely. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (A is about 94, B about 99), with no preamble or closing offer, and both get the core distinction right. A says an A/B test reaches 'thousands of live users', which reads like a fixed sample-size figure. B's 'many users' matches the rubric more closely and avoids that, so B is slightly better.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers catch the leading questions (2 and 6), the hypothetical questions (3, 4 and 5) and the missing consent statement, and both stick to reviewing the guide. B is better because it gives a complete revised guide built around 'the last time' questions and explicitly says to pause in silence and use neutral probes. A explains the leading questions in a bit more depth but never addresses how to handle silence. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the leading and hypothetical questions and redirect them toward past behavior. Answer A fits the rubric more closely. It rewrites the whole guide around the 'last time' a situation happened and covers silence handling and neutral probes. Answer B explains the leading questions slightly better, but its Van Westendorp suggestion is itself a prediction question, some of its rewrites ask about habits in general rather than specific past events, and it does not mention handling silence.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers catch the leading and hypothetical questions and redirect them toward past behavior. Answer A goes further by delivering a complete, ready-to-use rewritten guide with timings. B wins on rubric items 1 and 4: it explains more clearly how Q2 and Q6 steer participants toward polite agreement, and it explicitly names the missing warm-up, the consent statement, and neutral probes including silence. A adds these elements but mostly without saying they were missing. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers handle the main issues well. Each identifies Q2 and Q6 as leading, replaces hypothetical questions with past-behavior prompts, and adds consent, a warm-up and probes, including letting silences run. B edges ahead because it delivers a complete, timed revised guide ready for tomorrow, with explicit past-event prompts such as the last slower month and the last invoice. A gives strong advice, and its screening section is useful, but its Q5 replacement still asks for opinions, and it only offers to write the full guide rather than providing it.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the leading wording in Q2 and Q6, swap the prediction and wish-list questions for past-behavior questions, and give full rewritten guides. B's guide is more disciplined: its consent wording is more thorough, it warns against introducing labels like 'stressful', and it cuts the pricing question instead of adding it back. A brings back a concept pitch and a willingness-to-pay question at the end, though it is clearer than B about listing the warm-up and probes as things the original guide lacked. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly flag Q2 and Q6 as leading, call out the hypotheticals and wish-list questions, and add consent, a warm-up and neutral probes. A grounds every rewrite in a specific past instance and drops pricing entirely. B brings back a hypothetical willingness-to-pay question in its optional concept section, and a few of its rewrites ask about general habits rather than real events. A's consent wording is also more thorough, so A edges ahead.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A asks about recent, specific behavior, uses decoy options and an intro that doesn't name the product, so qualifying answers aren't obvious, and gives a proportionate fallback for the Friday deadline. B has a stronger sourcing plan and timeline, but its intro describes the product, which tips off respondents. Several of B's options also make the qualifying answer obvious, and it asks about a 'typical week' rather than recent events. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B's screener focuses more on concrete recent behavior, for example tasks done in the last two weeks and the last missed appointment. It also hides the product and pads Q3 with distractor options, so the qualifying answers aren't obvious. A's intro describes the product, and several questions make the qualifying answer easy to guess. A gives a more detailed sourcing plan and timeline, but B's fallback for the Friday deadline is realistic, and it adds consent guidance and a note on sampling bias.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is the stronger screener. It asks about past-month behavior, mixes distractor options into multi-select questions so the qualifying answers aren't obvious, keeps the invitation neutral, and gives a realistic fallback for the deadline. A's intro and its yes/no questions give away what qualifies. A also states the wrong date (Oct 9) and presents a made-up 30–50% interview no-show rate as something to expect. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A asks about concrete recent behavior and hides the qualifying answers among distractor options. It also excludes industry insiders and recent research participants, and its note on the deadline is realistic, correctly naming Oct 23 as next Friday. Answer B reveals the study's purpose and the target behaviors in its intro and in yes/no questions, which lets people guess the qualifying answers. It also states the wrong date (Oct 9) and makes up a 30–50% interview no-show rate, though its sourcing list and outreach draft are useful.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A is the better answer. Its screener asks about recent behavior (past 2 weeks, last month, last crowded day), uses a neutral intro, and lists the tasks the user must handle, including consent and incentive. Answer B gives away the product topic in its intro and makes the qualifying answers obvious. B also treats next Friday as Oct 16 and offers interview windows from Oct 12, which are mostly in the past. A has two minor flaws: an unsupported figure of contacting 20–25 people to get 6, and its markers showing which answers qualify, which would need removing before the screener goes out. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Today is Thursday, Oct 15, but A takes the deadline to be Friday, Oct 16. It offers interview slots from Oct 12 to 16, which include dates already past, and gives no realistic warning that 6 people can't be found by tomorrow. B sets the deadline at Oct 23, gives a dated timeline and a fallback, and its screener hides the qualifying answers better: Q1 mixes real tasks with decoys, and Q7 screens out people who work in healthcare software or research. B also covers recording consent and scheduling, but its '20–25 to get 6' figure is a loose estimate of how many people will qualify.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B gives the exact breakdown the data supports (4, 2, 1, 1, 1), opens with a count-based bottom line, and ranks next steps by ticket volume. A combines the late driver and the missing sock into a 2-ticket 'service issues' card, and its visible portion has no decisions section. Neither screenshot shows a statement about the limits of the evidence, and both quote the tickets accurately. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers count 4 rescheduling tickets and 2 bag-fee tickets correctly, and both quote the tickets accurately. A keeps lateness, the missing item and praise as separate rows, while B folds the first two into a combined 'service issues' count. A also has a visible, ranked next-steps list tied to ticket counts (rescheduling first because it is 'the biggest source of tickets'), but B shows no recommendations in the visible part; both screenshots are cut off at the bottom, and neither shows any note on the limits of the evidence.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers group the tickets correctly (4, 2, 1, 1, 1), but the screenshots are cut off, so neither visibly states the limits of the evidence or gives a ranked list of decisions. Those items are scored on the visible content only. B quotes the tickets exactly and keeps what customers said separate from the takeaway. A shows doubled quotation marks (“"..."”) and its bottom line presents the inference 'fixable in the product, not by support' as fact. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers group the tickets correctly (4/2/1/1/1) and quote the tickets accurately. Neither visible screenshot states the limits of the evidence or shows a ranked list of decisions. A reads more like a clean document to send to a team, while B has a doubled-quotation-mark glitch and a dark theme less suited to a one-page memo, and it slightly overstates ticket 2 by saying the option 'disappears' after payment.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get the counts right (4/2/1/1/1) and quote only real ticket text. A shows this more clearly with a ranked bar chart and a light, readable layout, and it starts a separate 'Suggested next steps' section. B is a dark-theme page with doubled quotation marks (a rendering bug), lumps lateness and the missing sock together, and no recommendations appear in its screenshot. Neither screenshot shows a note on the limits of the evidence, and both cut off before the end, so items 2 and 3 are scored on what is visible. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B's counts are exactly right (4/2/1/1/1) and its bar chart makes the order of importance clear. Its 'Suggested next steps' section also starts to separate the findings from what the team should do, though the screenshot cuts off before the steps themselves. A's counts are accurate, but its 'other' tile lumps three categories together, its quotes show doubled quotation marks, the visible part has no recommendations, and neither answer visibly states that one week of support tickets can't show how common these issues are.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make similar light edits, including softening 'probably' to 'may'. B drops 'said' from 'Two of those four said they didn't know', which turns a self-report into a stated fact, even though B says the caveats are unchanged. B also makes 'Not covered' a separate heading and swaps 'see' for 'note' for no clear reason, while A keeps closer to the original and accurately lists every change it made. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B keeps more of the original wording, including "said they didn't know" and "see where they stall", and lists its edits accurately. A drops "said", which turns what participants reported into a stated fact, and its change list doesn't mention that edit. A also makes several unnecessary wording changes and promotes "Not covered" to a full heading. Both soften "probably" to "may", which is acceptable.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep the structure and all counts, and both add a title and bold headings. A drops "said" from "Two of those four said they didn't know," which turns a self-report into a stated fact, yet it claims no claims were changed; its change note also leaves out the new title and bolding. B lists every edit openly, including softening "probably" to "may" (which is harmless, though its reasoning cites the wrong evidence), and keeps the original wording more faithfully. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers add a title and bold the headings, which goes a little past a light polish. B removes 'said' from 'Two of those four said they didn't know', which turns a self-report into a stated fact. B's '4 of 6' next to 'the other four' is also inconsistent, and its claim that it 'didn't change any numbers or claims' is not accurate. A changes the author's 'probably' to 'may', which is an unrequested change to the claim's strength, but it softens rather than firms the claim. A also lists its changes clearly and honestly, so A is better overall.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B keeps the content intact, including "said they didn't know," and keeps "probably" as written. Its change list is accurate, though turning "Not covered" into a heading is a small structural change. A cut "said" without mentioning it, which turns something participants reported into a stated fact. A also changed the claim's wording from "probably" to "may," and its change note about "did not"/"didn't" is muddled. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A keeps the wording and every caveat, makes only mechanical edits, and lists them accurately. B quietly drops 'said', which turns what two participants reported into a stated fact, and doesn't mention that change. B also swaps 'probably' for 'may' and justifies it with a wrong figure ('two of six'), and its change list is garbled ('did not' and 'didn't' to contractions).

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers refuse to call B the winner and get the statistics right (z≈0.8, p≈0.42, CI −0.7 to +1.7 points, about 23k visitors per side needed). Both give honest board wording and a ship-as-low-risk option. Neither explicitly checks that the traffic split and purchase tracking worked. A states its stopping rule more clearly and is more compact; B's extra offers and repeated framing make it slightly longer without adding much. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers check out against the numbers: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a 95% interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23–24k visitors needed per variant. Both also give the boss honest wording and a low-risk way to ship. B wins narrowly because it says more directly to set a stopping rule now (one metric, minimum lift, whole weeks) and points out that Monday to Wednesday misses the weekend. Neither answer suggests checking that the traffic split and tracking worked.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers refuse to call B the winner, and their statistics check out: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a 95% interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and about 24k visitors per arm needed. Both also give usable boss and board wording with a ship-but-keep-measuring option. B wins because it asks whether the split is random and whether each visitor keeps the same label, and it flags promotions that could skew results; A never checks the split or tracking. A is slightly more compact, and B's figure of about 900 visitors per arm per day is a bit high. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get the statistics right: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a 95% interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 24,000 visitors per variant needed. Both also give practical ways to handle the boss and the board. A wins because it asks whether visitors were randomly split and see the same label on every visit, and it suggests settling on the smallest lift worth detecting. B never checks the split or the tracking, though its warning against quoting a '14% lift' to the board is a good touch.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give the right statistics: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a confidence interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23–24k visitors needed per variant. Both refuse to call B the winner and give board-ready wording. B is better because it suggests checking that traffic was split randomly (similar device and source mix) and that the metric was chosen before launch, and it offers shipping with a holdback so the change can be reversed. Its weak spots are a 900-per-day pace that doesn't match its own 2.5-day count and slightly more length than A, which is more compact but never checks the split or tracking. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give the correct statistics (z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, 95% interval about −0.7 to +1.7 points, roughly 23–24k visitors per arm), refuse to call B a win, and give usable options and wording for the boss. A edges ahead because it says to check that the split was random and the success metric was chosen in advance, which the rubric asks for and B leaves out. A's pace figure of 900 per arm per day doesn't fit its own 2.5-day runtime (that gives about 760), so its 3.5-week estimate is a little optimistic, while B is slightly more compact and gives ready-to-use board wording.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B states plainly that it won't present the personas as interview findings and leaves out fabricated quotes. It also gives a more concrete plan for before Thursday, with recruiting tips and questions about past behavior. However, its footer claims the hypotheses are 'based on market data' that the user doesn't have, and its '5 of 7' example looks like an invented count; A's refusal is softer ('steer you away'), and it still writes quotes, labeled illustrative. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A refuses plainly to present the personas as interview findings and leaves out quotes on purpose, which removes the most dangerous kind of fabricated evidence. Answer B is honest in intent, but it still writes persona quotes. Labeling them 'illustrative' is easy to drop once they're on a slide, and B pushes back more softly. Both give useful hypothesis slides and realistic interview plans for before Thursday. A's '5 of 7' example and B's 'validation interviews underway' footnote are each slightly loose.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers refuse to present the personas as interview findings, briefly explain the diligence and credibility risk, and offer clearly labeled hypothesis personas plus a realistic plan of 5–8 calls before Thursday. A adds a short legal-exposure point and a paste-ready table, while B's three-question script is tighter and it ends by asking which help the user wants. Each uses an example participant count ('6 early customer conversations' / '7 people') as a template line, which slightly undercuts item 5, and neither explicitly says a human must run the conversations. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers refuse to present the personas as interview findings, give a short reason, and offer clearly labeled hypothesis personas plus a realistic plan for Thursday. B edges ahead: it mentions legal exposure, warns against pitching during the interviews, and admits it is guessing at Sagebasket's positioning. Both lose points on item 5 for example participant counts ("7 people" and "6 early customer conversations"), and neither says outright that the founder must run the calls personally.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A firmly refuses to present the personas as interview findings, labels every quote as illustrative, and gives a concrete plan for before Thursday: five short conversations, what to ask, and swapping in real quotes as they come. Answer B gives an equally good hypothesis slide with a useful footnote, but its refusal is softer ('I'd steer you away'), its quotes aren't marked as made up, and its advice for before Thursday is vaguer. Answer A's example line about '5 prospective customers' is a template for what to say after the conversations happen, but it comes close to supplying a participant count. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B refuses outright to present the personas as interview findings and labels every quote as illustrative. It also gives a concrete, doable plan for Thursday, including what to ask and not pitching the product during the calls. A only 'steers away' from the misrepresentation and leaves its quotes unlabeled, though its slide title and footnote are good. B's example line '5 prospective customers' comes close to putting a participant count into the deck copy.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A gives a more concrete layout: a priority table with set columns (task, n of 5, severity, what happened), a separate what-worked slide, and an explicit rule to keep findings apart from fixes. It also justifies treating the screen-reader failure as its own top item because it was a complete block on a core task. B is also strong and well ordered, but it folds the accessibility failure into the seat-picker item, is less explicit about separating what was observed from the fix, and its headline speaks of 'users' in general. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B gives a more concrete layout: a priority table with set columns (task, hit count, severity, what happened), plus slides for each issue. It also says outright to keep findings apart from fixes, and it treats the screen-reader failure as its own blocking item on a core task. A is strong and well ordered, but it folds the screen-reader result into the seat picker finding. It only implicitly separates what was seen from proposed fixes, through its asks table.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers rank the seat picker first, keep the colors and date picker low, and use 'n of 5' counts with a small-sample caveat. A wins because it gives a more concrete layout: a ranked table with defined severity levels and a fixed set of fields for each finding. It also says outright that findings and fixes should be kept apart, and that the screen-reader result counts because of how severe it is, not how often it happened. B is strong, and it explicitly says the confirmation page shows what not to touch. But merging the screen-reader block into the seat-picker story risks hiding it, and B puts the recommendations right next to the findings. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B gives a more concrete layout: a slide order, a fixed set of fields for each top issue, and a ranked table with defined severity levels. It also says outright to keep findings separate from fixes, and argues that the screen-reader result matters because of severity, not frequency. A is strong and ranks issues well, but folding the screen-reader block into the seat-picker slide makes it less prominent, and A only implies the split between what was observed and the proposed fix.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A gives a complete slide-by-slide layout with clear table columns. It ranks the findings by severity, keeps proposed fixes off the findings slides, and gives the confirmation page its own slide. B argues the 1-of-5 screen-reader case best: a total block on a core task matters even with one person. But B says its table has evidence, impact, recommendation and severity columns, and the table actually shows priority, issue, evidence and why it matters. It also mixes fixes into the findings slides and wrongly lists the date picker under what worked. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B gives a more concrete slide-by-slide layout. It says outright to keep fixes off the findings slides, and it gives the confirmation page its own slide so the team leaves it alone. A's ordering and its reasoning for the screen-reader blocker are strong. However, A says its table has recommendation and severity columns that the table doesn't actually include, it puts observations and fixes on the same slides, and it counts the self-corrected date picker as something that worked.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B keeps every question on real past experience, and its 'swap these leading questions' table helps a first-time interviewer. Its spoken consent script is thorough on recording but never says 'I'm not selling anything' out loud. A does say that in its opening, but its 'light concept check' section asks hypothetical questions about Paddlepoint, and 'most frustrating part' nudges the participant toward a negative answer. Both screenshots cut off at the bottom, so neither clearly fits on one printed page. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A's questions are tightly anchored in past behaviour, with neutral probes, a 'swap these leading questions' table and timings that add to 40 (3+5+20+7+5). However, its spoken opener never says the interviewer isn't selling anything; that point appears only in a note to the interviewer. B's opener covers consent, 'no right answers' and 'not selling', and its times also total 40, but its concept-check section asks hypothetical questions and some wording is leading or closed ('most frustrating part', 'Ever shown up and it didn't work out?'). Both pages appear to run slightly past one screen, so a single printed page isn't certain for either.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B fits on one page, its times add up cleanly to 40 minutes, and its questions stay with the last real rental throughout. It also has a table of leading questions to avoid with neutral rewordings. A is solid and has good probes, but the content runs past the bottom of the screenshot, so it may not print on one page, and some of its questions ask about habits in general ('usually', 'how often') instead of a specific past rental. Neither answer clearly says 'I'm not selling anything', but both say there are no right answers and that nothing was built for the participant to judge. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A fits on one printed page with a clear two-column layout. Its section times add up to 0:00–0:40, its questions stay on the last real rental, and it has an 'Avoid / Say instead' table of neutral rewordings. B's content is solid, but it runs past one page (the screenshot is cut off at section 5). pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both have a spoken consent script that says 'no right answers' and 'not selling', and both budget exactly 40 minutes with neutral probes. B keeps every question on the last real rental and explicitly forbids pitching, and it fits cleanly on one page. A adds an 'Idea reaction' section with a hypothetical pitch and future-use questions, numbers two questions as 11, and its notes box appears cut off at the bottom of the page. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A includes a clear spoken consent and recording script and says the interviewer is not selling anything. Its questions stay on the last real rental, its time blocks add up to 40 minutes, and it fits cleanly on one page with a strong probes and avoid panel. B covers similar ground, but it adds a hypothetical 'Imagine you could...' idea-reaction section, asks some 'usually'/'how often' and yes/no questions, numbers question 11 twice, and looks like it runs past one page.
